title: Conversation Shortcuts — feature notes and rough PRD
body:
Context:

Quick brain dump about a lightweight feature I keep sketching in meeting after meeting: 'Conversation Shortcuts' — a way for end users to pin or invoke pre-built mini-flows and canned context for common tasks inside long-running conversations.

Why now:
- Customer feedback: CS reported multiple customers asking for ways to 'jump back' to a common template (e.g., legal summary, TL;DR, persona switch) without re-sending large context every time.
- Cost/latency: many apps rebuild context repeatedly when users want to re-run a known subtask (e.g., extract entities). We can reduce tokens and GPU time by storing compacted representations and rerunning only the minimal prompt.
- Competitive: similar UX found in other chat apps, but we can differentiate by exposing fidelity controls and cost signals to users and having server-side compact snapshots.

One-line idea:
- Let users create / discover 'shortcuts' inside a conversation: a saved sub-prompt + optional small context snapshot + preferred model/quality setting. Users can apply it to the current thread with a single click.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Increase repeatable task efficiency: common subtask latency reduced by 20–40% on average.
- User adoption: 10–15% of active conversation users try a shortcut within 6 weeks of exposure in an experimental cohort.
- Cost: reduce redundant token throughput for targeted workflows (customer support macros, legal summarize, code rewrite) by at least 30% per action.

Non-goals:
- Not a full macro automation engine (not running multi-step orchestrations yet).
- Not replacing external tool integrations (Zapier etc.).

High-level design options (brainstorm):
1) Client-only shortcuts (quickest): UI stores the prompt template locally (browser/localStorage); when invoked the client injects template into the live convo and sends full prompt. Pros: easiest. Cons: still token-expensive, no centralized discoverability.

2) Server-side compact snapshots + tokenized template: store a compacted representation (prefix KV cache or condensed prompt) keyed to conversation + shortcut ID. When invoked, the server routes the request through a fast-path that uses cached KV state to avoid re-encoding the whole conversation. Pros: big token savings, lower latency. Cons: more infra work, SRE/consistency considerations.

3) Model-aware fidelity profiles: allow the shortcut to specify a target model variant (e.g., cheap quantized 4-bit for extraction, full model for final summaries) and an automatic fallback policy. Integrates with Redwood Optimize suggestions.

Suggested MVP (hybrid):
- Start with server-side templates + cheap 'compact snapshot' heuristic: store last N key messages compressed into a 1–2 KB snapshot string. Shortcut application prepends snapshot + template and uses a dedicated route that sets batching hint and smaller max_tokens for that flow. No KV cache plumbing in MVP.
- UI: shortcut create/edit modal, small gallery inside conversation (top-right), quick keyboard shortcut (e.g., /shortcut).

User personas & user stories:
- Support agent (small SaaS): 'As a support agent, I want a "bug triage" shortcut that extracts OS, stack, and error codes from user messages so I can paste a draft into ticketing quickly.'
- Legal counsel (enterprise): 'As a lawyer, I want a "contract-clause-scan" shortcut that looks at a pasted clause and highlights risky language with a short rationale.'
- Developer (internal): 'As an engineer, I want a "refactor-suggestion" shortcut to run selected code through a concise micro-eval that only returns transformed code and minimal explanation.'

Acceptance criteria (MVP):
- Users can create/edit/delete shortcuts in the conversation UI.
- Shortcut application triggers a single server call and returns results within configured latency SLO (e.g., p95 < 800ms for cheap-extraction flow).
- Shortcut runs use <= 60% of tokens compared to full-context recompose in pilot workloads (measured on 5 sample customers).
- Telemetry events emitted: shortcut_create, shortcut_invoke, shortcut_delete, shortcut_invoke_latency, shortcut_invoke_cost_estimate.

Telemetry / metrics to track:
- Adoption funnel: impressions -> create -> first invoke -> repeat invoke (per-user).
- Token delta per invocation (tokens sent without shortcut vs with shortcut).
- Latency distribution by shortcut type and model chosen.
- Cost delta (estimated GPU-tokens saved) and customer-visible cost signal (if we surface it).

Security / privacy considerations:
- Shortcuts may store small snapshots of conversation. We need explicit UI copy and an opt-out. For private deployments, default to store shortcuts in customer-managed DB or local-only.
- Evaluate whether snapshots count as customer data for retention/SARs. Flag this with Legal (linked JIRA above).

Rollout idea / experiment plan:
- Phase A (internal beta): enable for Redwood staff only, collect qualitative feedback.
- Phase B (pilot customers): 3 enterprise customers (CS-led), monitor token reduction and UX friction.
- Phase C (A/B test in hosted product): show a small gallery suggestion to a randomized user segment and measure adoption + cost delta.

Short UX sketches (notes, not designs):
- Shortcut card shows: name, short description, model hint dot (green=cheap, orange=balanced), times-used badge.
- Quick apply: hover -> "Apply" -> small inline preview before sending.
- Create flow: name, description, category (extract/transform/summarize), attached snapshot toggle (on/off), model preference dropdown, cost hint toggle (show estimate).

Engineering considerations / dependencies:
- Storage for shortcuts (user-scoped and conversation-scoped) — small schema.
- Fast-path route that accepts a shortcut ID and a minimal invocation payload (message id or selection).
- Telemetry and billing hook to estimate token savings per-call.
- Admin controls for private deployments (local storage option).

Open questions / tradeoffs (TODO):
- Snapshot format: plain text vs tokenized compressed state vs real KV cache. How much infra complexity justified for 1st iteration?
- UX discoverability vs noise: do we show suggestions proactively or keep behind a menu?
- How to let users share shortcuts across teams/orgs and control visibility? (org vs personal scopes)
- How to price or surface cost-savings: free optimization vs premium feature for dedicated customers?

Notes to self / quick TODOs:
- Talk to Evan about telemetry shape + RED-4127 details (cost calc work).
- Ask Maya for a rough UI frame I can prototype in Figma — aim for 3 screens.
- Reach out to SRE to discuss fast-path route implications and request a spike estimate (1–2w).
- Draft initial e2e playbook for pilot customers: sample prompts, scripts, success criteria.

Small example flows (copyable):
- Shortcut: "Extract metadata"
  - Snapshot: last two user messages (trim to 512 chars)
  - Template: "Extract OS, browser, and error code. Return as JSON keys: os, browser, error_code, short_summary."
  - Model hint: small extraction model (gpt-4o-mini)
\- Invocation: user selects a message -> hit /shortcut -> choose "Extract metadata" -> server returns JSON output.

Risks:
- If shortcuts are too powerful and stored centrally we introduce new attack surface for data leakage (malicious saved prompts referencing sensitive fields). Need sanitization and proper permissions.
- Complexity creep: this can quickly expand into a macro/orchestration product we are not equipped to support right away.

Next steps (this week):
- Stub a short prototype on the hosted UI (client-only) to validate UX in 2 days.
- Legal check on snapshot storage implications (open a quick Jira if needed).
- Quick performance test: simulate 1000 shortcut invokes with small snapshot vs full recomposition and measure token delta using Redwood bench harness.

Long-term vision (brainstorm):
- Make shortcuts first-class automation building blocks: chain them, schedule them, expose them in the Redwood Console for org admins, and tie into Optimize to recommend shortcuts automatically for repeatable sequences.

General tone: this is a lightweight, product-facing feature that sits between simple canned responses and full orchestration. The sweet spot is high-frequency, low-complexity tasks where token and latency savings are meaningful and user productivity increases.

-- Noemie
